etymology: From Anglo-Saxon spittan, to eject saliva from the mouth. Webster 1828: to throw out saliva from the mouth. In Scripture the act is almost never merely physical; it is the body’s shorthand for contempt, and the law made it a formal sign of disgrace (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9).
biblical_def: Of all the indignities laid on the Lord Jesus, spitting is the one He named in advance and the one Isaiah saw seven centuries early. I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). The Servant does not merely endure the insult; He declines to hide from it. Christ repeats the prophecy as a plain itinerary: they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again (Mark 10:34) — and the Sanhedrin fulfils it word for word: Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him (Matthew 26:67). Understand what the face is in Hebrew thought. To seek God’s face is to seek His favour; to have Him hide His face is judgment. Men spat on the face of God incarnate. Yet the same Lord had used spittle as a means of mercy: he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man (John 9:6). What man aimed at Him in contempt, He had already turned toward man in healing — the exchange the whole gospel runs on.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPIT as to eject or throw out saliva from the mouth; and notes the biblical usage in which spitting on a person is the extreme public token of contempt and rejection.
webster_full: SPIT, v.t. — To eject from the mouth; to throw out, as saliva.
SPIT, v.i. — To throw out saliva from the mouth.
To spit in or on the face, in the Scriptures, is a mark of the deepest contempt and abhorrence.
SPITTLE, n. — The moist matter of the mouth; saliva.
Anglo-Saxon spittan, spatl, saliva; connected with spew and sputter.
scriptures: Isaiah 50:6
I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
Mark 10:34
And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again.
Matthew 26:67
Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him; and others smote him with the palms of their hands,
John 9:6
When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay,
corruption_summary: A sentimental modern piety keeps the cross solemn but scrubs it of squalor, and in doing so it loses the doctrine: it was shame, not only pain, that the Servant bore.
corruption_paragraphs: Preaching that dwells on the physical mechanics of crucifixion while passing quickly over the spitting has the emphasis backwards. Isaiah 53 puts contempt at the centre — despised and rejected of men — and the spitting is contempt made visible. The Reformed doctrine of Christ’s humiliation (the state of humiliation, running from the incarnation to the burial) holds that our Lord bore not only the penalty of sin but its disgrace. The 1689 Confession speaks of Him enduring most grievous torments in His soul and most painful sufferings in His body; the soul-torment is the harder half, and being spat upon by the creatures He made is a fair sample of it. Any account of the atonement that treats the cross as a transaction in pain alone has not reckoned with the face that men spat upon.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exchange at the heart of the gospel. Christ received on His face what our sin deserved, and used spittle from that same mouth to open a blind man’s eyes. He was shamed that we might be honoured; He was rejected that we might be received. Numbers 12:14 shows the weight of the sign — if a father had but spit in his daughter’s face, she would bear the shame seven days. The Son bore the Father’s face turned away and men’s spittle upon His own, and did not hide.
roots_summary: Hebrew roq (H7536), spittle; yaraq (H3417), to spit; Greek emptuo (G1716), to spit upon; ptuo (G4429), to spit; ptusma (G4427), spittle.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaraq (H3417) — to spit; used of the formal disgrace in Deuteronomy 25:9 and Numbers 12:14.
Hebrew roq (H7536) — spittle; I hid not my face from shame and spitting (Isaiah 50:6).
Greek emptuo (G1716) — to spit upon, the compound of en (upon) and ptuo; used of the Passion in Matthew 26:67 and Mark 10:34.
Greek ptuo (G4429) — to spit; used of the Lord’s healing act in John 9:6.
Greek ptusma (G4427) — spittle, the noun behind the clay our Lord made in John 9:6.
usage: I hid not my face from shame and spitting (Isaiah 50:6) — the Servant does not merely endure the insult; He declines to hide from it.
Then did they spit in his face (Matthew 26:67) — the face of God incarnate, and the face is where favour lives in Hebrew thought.
He spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle (John 9:6) — what men aimed at Him in contempt, He had already turned toward man in healing.

etymology: From Middle English wrappen, to fold or wind about, of uncertain Germanic origin. Webster 1828: to wind or fold together; to involve; to cover by winding something round. Scripture uses it at the two ends of our Lord’s earthly life — the swaddling bands and the grave clothes.
biblical_def: The word binds the manger to the tomb. Luke records the nativity in the plainest terms: she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger (Luke 2:7), and the angel makes those bands the appointed evidence: Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger (Luke 2:12). The sign of the Messiah is not a crown but a cloth. Thirty-three years later John looks into an empty sepulchre and notices how the linen lay: the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself (John 20:7). The detail is evidential. A robbed grave is a ransacked grave; this one is orderly, the head-cloth folded by itself, as of a man who rose and had no need of haste. Between manger and tomb the word appears in Jonah’s prayer from the deep: the weeds were wrapped about my head (Jonah 2:5) — and our Lord Himself made Jonah’s three days the one sign He would give. He who was wrapped in swaddling bands was wrapped in grave clothes, and left them folded.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WRAP as to wind or fold together; to involve; to cover by winding or folding something about a thing; hence WRAPPED, involved, enveloped, folded about.
webster_full: WRAP, v.t. — To wind or fold together; as, to wrap close.
To involve; to cover by winding or folding something round.
To comprise; to contain; as, this is wrapped up in the general question.
WRAPPED, pp. — Wound; folded; enveloped; involved.
Middle English wrappen; compare lap, to fold, and envelop.
scriptures: Luke 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
Luke 2:12
And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.
John 20:7
And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.
Jonah 2:5
The waters compassed me about, even to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head.
corruption_summary: Modern nativity sentiment turns the swaddling clothes into a picture of cosiness; Scripture makes them a sign of humiliation, and the folded napkin of John 20:7 a sober evidence of resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: The swaddling bands are not decoration. They are the first article of the Son’s humiliation after the incarnation itself: the eternal Word, by whom the worlds were made, bound in cloth like any other infant and laid where beasts feed. Luke names the reason without softening it — because there was no room for them in the inn. When the carol tradition turns this into rustic charm, the doctrine goes out of it. The angel gave the bands as the identifying sign: the shepherds would know Messiah not by splendour but by poverty. That is the pattern of the whole ministry, and the 1689 Confession states it plainly in its chapter on the mediator — He took our nature with all its essential properties and common infirmities, yet without sin.

John 20:7 has been pressed by some into ingenious readings about ancient napkin-folding customs; the text needs no such help. The evidential point is simply order. Grave-robbers do not unwind a body and leave the head-cloth folded apart. John saw it, and the next verse says he believed. The Reformed doctrine of the resurrection rests on bodily, public, examinable fact — the same body that was wrapped, now risen — not on the disciples’ inner experience. Any account that relocates the resurrection into the believer’s subjectivity has abandoned what John reports himself to have looked at and handled.
roots_summary: Greek sparganoo (G4683), to wrap in swaddling bands; entulisso (G1794), to wrap up, to roll together; Hebrew chabash (H2280), to bind or wrap about.
roots_lines: Greek sparganoo (G4683) — to swathe in strips of cloth; used only of the infant Christ, in Luke 2:7 and Luke 2:12.
Greek entulisso (G1794) — to roll or fold together; used of the head napkin in John 20:7.
Greek eneileo (G1750) — to wind in, used by Mark of the linen at the burial (Mark 15:46).
Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind, to wrap about; used of Jonah’s weeds and of binding up wounds.
Hebrew suph (H5488) — weeds or reeds, the sea-growth wrapped about Jonah’s head (Jonah 2:5).
usage: Wrapped him in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:7) — the first article of the Son’s humiliation after the incarnation itself.
Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:12) — the appointed sign of Messiah is a cloth, not a crown.
Wrapped together in a place by itself (John 20:7) — a robbed grave is ransacked; this one is orderly.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon dyppan, to plunge into a liquid and withdraw. Webster 1828: to plunge or immerse for a moment in a liquid. In the Levitical system it is a priestly action word: the finger, the hyssop, the bird, all dipped in blood or water before anything is applied.
biblical_def: Nothing in the sanctuary was applied dry. The priest must first dip, and what he dips into is blood: the priest shall dip his finger in the blood, and sprinkle of the blood seven times before the LORD, before the vail of the sanctuary (Leviticus 4:6). The order is fixed and it is doctrine — contact with the blood precedes every application of it. Israel’s deliverance began the same way, with a bunch of hyssop: ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts (Exodus 12:22). The blood in the basin saved no one; the blood applied to the door did. Naaman learned the lesson against his pride: then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean (2 Kings 5:14) — cleansing by an appointed means, in an unimpressive river, at a prophet’s bare word. And John sees the King return with the action already accomplished on Himself: he was clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God (Revelation 19:13).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DIP as to plunge or immerse for a moment or short time in water or other liquid substance; to take by dipping; to wet, as with a liquid.
webster_full: DIP, v.t. — To plunge or immerse, for a moment or short time, in water or other liquid substance.
To take with a ladle or other vessel by immersing it in a fluid; as, to dip water from a boiler.
To engage as a pledge; to take a concern in.
DIP, v.i. — To sink; to enter; to incline downward.
Anglo-Saxon dyppan, to dip; related to deep and to baptize in its plain sense of plunging.
scriptures: Leviticus 4:6
And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood, and sprinkle of the blood seven times before the LORD, before the vail of the sanctuary.
Exodus 12:22

And ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts with the blood that is in the bason; and none of you shall go out at the door of his house until the morning.
2 Kings 5:14
Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
Revelation 19:13
And he was clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God.
corruption_summary: The plain sense of dipping — plunging and withdrawing — is the sense of the New Testament word for baptism, and every argument for sprinkling as the mode has to work against the vocabulary rather than with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Dip is the ordinary English for what bapto and baptizo describe, and Naaman in Jordan is the Old Testament picture the New Testament vocabulary reaches for. This dictionary holds believer’s baptism by immersion as the New Testament pattern, and the lexical point is a large part of the reason: the Greek word means to plunge, and every attempt to make it mean an application of a few drops must be argued around the word rather than from it. The 1689 Confession states it directly — immersion, the dipping of the person in water, is necessary to the due administration of the ordinance. Note also who is dipped: Naaman went down himself, at the word of God, having first been offended that the means were so plain. That is the order of faith, and infant baptism cannot reproduce it.

There is a second corruption to name, subtler and more common among the orthodox: treating the blood of Christ as sufficient in the basin. Exodus 12 is emphatic that the blood in the bason saved nobody in Egypt; the blood on the lintel did. The Reformed doctrine of the application of redemption — effectual calling, union with Christ, justification by faith — is exactly this insistence that what Christ purchased must be applied by the Spirit to the individual soul. A general atonement floating unapplied over mankind is a bason of blood and an unmarked door. Definite atonement says the Lamb was slain for His people and the blood is certainly struck on every door He purchased.
roots_summary: Hebrew tabal (H2881), to dip, to immerse; Greek bapto (G911), to dip, to dye by dipping; baptizo (G907), to immerse, to submerge.
roots_lines: Hebrew tabal (H2881) — to dip or plunge; used of the priest’s finger (Leviticus 4:6), the hyssop (Exodus 12:22), and Naaman in Jordan (2 Kings 5:14).
Greek bapto (G911) — to dip, and so to dye by dipping; used of the vesture dipped in blood (Revelation 19:13).
Greek baptizo (G907) — the intensive form, to immerse or submerge; the New Testament word for the ordinance.
Hebrew ezob (H231) — hyssop, the bunch used to carry the blood from bason to lintel (Exodus 12:22).
Hebrew nazah (H5137) — to sprinkle, the action that follows the dipping (Leviticus 4:6).
usage: The priest shall dip his finger in the blood (Leviticus 4:6) — contact with the blood precedes every application of it.
Dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel (Exodus 12:22) — the blood in the basin saved no one; the blood applied did.
He dipped himself seven times in Jordan (2 Kings 5:14) — cleansing by an appointed means, at a prophet’s bare word.

etymology: From Middle English tip, the point or extremity of a thing, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: the end or point of a thing, especially a small extremity. In Scripture it is a word of consecration: the blood of the ram is put on the tip of the ear, the thumb, and the great toe.
biblical_def: The word appears where God is most particular, and the particularity is the point. At the ordination of Aaron and his sons, Moses is commanded: put it upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron, and upon the tip of the right ear of his sons, and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot (Exodus 29:20). Three places, and each one a faculty: the ear that must hear the word of God, the hand that must do the work of God, the foot that must walk in the ways of God. Blood on all three means a man wholly claimed — hearing, doing, walking — and none of it his own. The identical rite cleanses the healed leper: the priest shall put it upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot (Leviticus 14:14; so also Leviticus 14:25). The restored outcast is consecrated by the same blood as the high priest, which is a very great mercy set in a very small detail. The word turns up once more, terribly, in the mouth of a man past mercy: send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue (Luke 16:24). In hell the request is reduced to a fingertip, and even that is refused.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TIP as the end; the point or extremity of anything small; as the tip of the finger, the tip of the ear.
webster_full: TIP, n. — The end; the point or extremity of any thing small; as the tip of the finger.
A piece put on the end of a thing; as the tip of a staff.
TIP, v.t. — To form a point upon; to cover the tip or end.
To strike slightly, or with the end of a thing.
Middle English tip; compare top, the upper extremity.
scriptures: Exodus 29:20

Then shalt thou kill the ram, and take of his blood, and put it upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron, and upon the tip of the right ear of his sons, and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot, and sprinkle the blood upon the altar round about.
Leviticus 14:14

And the priest shall take some of the blood of the trespass offering, and the priest shall put it upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot:
Leviticus 14:25

And he shall kill the lamb of the trespass offering, and the priest shall take some of the blood of the trespass offering, and put it upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot:
Luke 16:24
And he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.
corruption_summary: Levitical detail is routinely dismissed as primitive ritual; in fact the ear, thumb and toe are a doctrine of whole-person consecration that the New Testament never repeals but universalizes.
corruption_paragraphs: The habit of reading Leviticus as an anthropological curiosity — the residue of an ancient Near Eastern cult — is one of the standing defaults of modern academic treatment, and it is a corruption of the text’s own claim. Leviticus presents itself as the LORD speaking out of the tabernacle, and its details are not arbitrary. Blood on ear, thumb and toe is a deliberate anatomy of obedience: what a man hears, what a man does, where a man goes. Paul preaches precisely this when he begs believers to present their bodies a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1), and Peter applies the priestly language to the whole church (1 Peter 2:9). The Levitical rite is not superseded into irrelevance; it is fulfilled in Christ and then extended to every believer.

Luke 16:24 must be allowed to say what it says. The rich man is conscious, articulate, in torment, and beyond remedy, and his request has shrunk to the tip of a finger dipped in water. This dictionary holds eternal conscious punishment and rejects annihilationism, universalism, and every post-mortem second chance. Abraham’s answer names a great gulf fixed — fixed, not provisional. The sentimental instinct that God’s love would not permit such an end is not an argument from Scripture but against it, and it is the same instinct that, followed further, empties the cross of necessity. If the smallest mercy can be refused there, the largest mercy offered here is not to be trifled with.
roots_summary: Hebrew tenuk (H8571), the tip or lobe of the ear; bohen (H931), thumb or great toe; Greek akron (G206), the extremity or tip.
roots_lines: Hebrew tenuk (H8571) — the lobe or tip of the ear; used only in the consecration and cleansing rites (Exodus 29:20; Leviticus 8:23; Leviticus 14:14).
Hebrew bohen (H931) — the thumb of the hand or the great toe of the foot, both anointed with the same blood.
Greek akron (G206) — the extremity, the topmost or farthest point; the tip of his finger (Luke 16:24).
Hebrew male yad — to fill the hand, the idiom for consecration to priestly office (Exodus 29:9).
Hebrew asham (H817) — the trespass offering whose blood is applied to the cleansed leper (Leviticus 14:14).
usage: Upon the tip of the right ear... the thumb... the great toe (Exodus 29:20) — the ear that hears, the hand that works, the foot that walks, all claimed by blood.
Upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed (Leviticus 14:14) — the restored outcast consecrated by the same blood as the high priest.
That he may dip the tip of his finger in water (Luke 16:24) — in hell the request is reduced to a fingertip, and even that is refused.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon holh, a hole or cavity. Webster 1828: containing an empty space within; not solid. Scripture uses it three ways: the cupped hand of God, the socket of a thigh, and the deliberate emptiness of the altar.
biblical_def: Isaiah’s great taunt against idolatry begins with a hand: Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure? (Isaiah 40:12). Every ocean is a palmful. The verse is not poetry decorating a doctrine; it is the doctrine — divine immensity stated in a household measure so that the mind can feel the disproportion before the chapter turns to ask, To whom then will ye liken God? The same word marks the night Jacob was crippled into a prince: he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him (Genesis 32:25). God wins by touching a socket, and the man who prevailed walked lame for the rest of his life. Third, the altar itself was built empty: Hollow with boards shalt thou make it: as it was shewed thee in the mount, so shall they make it (Exodus 27:8) — the place of sacrifice is a frame around a void, filled by what God provides, not by what men supply. And when Samson was dying of thirst, God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw, and there came water thereout; and when he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived (Judges 15:19).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HOLLOW as containing an empty space, natural or artificial, within a solid substance; not solid; and as a noun, a cavity, a depression, a hole.
webster_full: HOLLOW, a. — Containing an empty space, natural or artificial, within a solid substance; not solid.
Sunk deep in the orbit; as a hollow eye.
Deep; low; resembling sound reverberated from a cavity; as a hollow groan.
HOLLOW, n. — A cavity; a depression of the surface of anything; a hole; a den.
Anglo-Saxon holh, a hollow place; connected with hole and hell in its older sense of a covered place.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:12

Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?
Genesis 32:25
And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob's thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him.
Exodus 27:8
Hollow with boards shalt thou make it: as it was shewed thee in the mount, so shall they make it.
Judges 15:19
But God clave an hollow place that was in the jaw, and there came water thereout; and when he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived
corruption_summary: Isaiah 40:12 is the standing rebuke to every theology that shrinks God to a manageable size, whether by open theism’s limited foreknowledge or by process theology’s developing deity.
corruption_paragraphs: The God who holds the seas in a cupped hand is not the God of open theism, and the difference is not a matter of emphasis. Open theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge, making God a very great being who is nonetheless learning; process theology goes further and denies immutability and omnipotence outright, making God a partner in becoming. Isaiah 40 forecloses both. The chapter’s argument runs from the hollow of the hand to the nations as a drop of a bucket to the taunt To whom then will ye liken God? — and the answer required is: to nothing and to no one. Classical theism, with its aseity, immutability and impassibility, is not a Greek intrusion on the Hebrew Bible, as is often asserted; it is Isaiah 40 stated in the vocabulary of the schools.

Genesis 32:25 corrects a different error, the sentimental doctrine that God’s blessing leaves a man intact. Jacob wrestles, prevails, and is maimed in the same night, and the maiming is part of the blessing — he limps away with a new name. The Puritans made much of this and were right to. Sanctification is not the improvement of a man’s native strength but often the disabling of it, so that he leans. Any teaching that promises the believer power without breaking, victory without a limp, is not describing the God who touched the hollow of Jacob’s thigh.
roots_summary: Hebrew shoal (H8168), the hollow of the hand, a handful; kaph (H3709), the palm or socket; nabab (H5014), to be hollow; maktesh (H4388), a mortar or hollow place.
roots_lines: Hebrew shoal (H8168) — the hollow of the hand as a measure; the waters in the hollow of his hand (Isaiah 40:12).
Hebrew kaph (H3709) — the palm, and by extension any socket or hollow; used of Jacob’s thigh (Genesis 32:25).
Hebrew nabab (H5014) — to hollow out, to make empty; the altar made hollow with boards (Exodus 27:8).
Hebrew maktesh (H4388) — a hollow or mortar; the hollow place in the jaw at Lehi (Judges 15:19).
Hebrew zereth (H2239) — the span, the companion measure to the hollow hand in Isaiah 40:12.
usage: The waters in the hollow of his hand (Isaiah 40:12) — every ocean a palmful; divine immensity in a household measure.
He touched the hollow of his thigh (Genesis 32:25) — God wins by touching a socket, and the victor walks lame.
Hollow with boards shalt thou make it (Exodus 27:8) — the place of sacrifice is a frame around a void.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hleapan, to run, to spring. Webster 1828: to spring or rise from the ground with both feet, as man; to jump; to bound. In Scripture leaping is nearly always involuntary joy — the body outrunning the will.
biblical_def: Isaiah puts leaping in the middle of his picture of the age to come, and it is a healing image before it is a happy one: Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert (Isaiah 35:6). Not merely walk — leap as an hart, with the surplus energy of a creature that was never lame. Luke, a physician, records the literal fulfilment with a threefold verb that will not be hurried: he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God (Acts 3:8). The man is forty years old and has never once walked; he does not learn to, he simply leaps. Earlier in the same Gospel, the first person to recognize the incarnate Christ does so before birth: when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost (Luke 1:41). John the Baptist begins his ministry as a forerunner in utero. And our Lord commands the affection under persecution: Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for, behold, your reward is great in heaven (Luke 6:23).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LEAP as to spring or rise from the ground with both feet, as man; to jump; to vault; to bound; to skip; and figuratively, to rush with vehemence.
webster_full: LEAP, v.i. — To spring or rise from the ground with both feet, as man, or with all the feet, as other animals; to jump; to vault.
To rush with violence; as, to leap upon a person.
To spring or bound with joy; as, the heart leaps with gladness.
LEAP, n. — A jump; a spring; a bound; a sudden transition.
Anglo-Saxon hleapan, to run or leap; whence gallop and lope.
scriptures: Isaiah 35:6
Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.
Acts 3:8
And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God.
Luke 1:41
And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost:
Luke 6:23
Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for, behold, your reward is great in heaven: for in the like manner did their fathers unto the prophets.
corruption_summary: Luke 1:41 says a six-month unborn child recognized his Lord and leaped, and no argument for the disposability of the unborn survives an honest reading of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Elisabeth’s child is at roughly six months’ gestation, and Luke — a physician writing an orderly account — ascribes to him perception, response and joy. The Greek is brephos, the ordinary word for a baby, and Luke uses the very same word two chapters later for the newborn Christ in the manger (Luke 2:12, 2:16). Scripture makes no vocabulary distinction between the child in the womb and the child in the arms. Add Psalm 139:13-16, where God covers David in his mother’s womb and writes his days in a book before one of them exists, and Jeremiah 1:5, where the prophet is known and sanctified before he is formed. The modern legal category that grants personhood at a chosen threshold is not a discovery about biology but a decision about whose image-bearing will be recognized, and Genesis 1:27 is the standard the dictionary holds against it.

There is a smaller corruption to name in Luke 6:23, and it runs the opposite way from the usual complaint about joyless religion. Our Lord commands leaping — but the occasion He commands it for is being hated, separated, reproached and cast out for the Son of man’s sake. Modern worship vocabulary has learned to speak of exuberance detached from any such setting, as though the leaping were the point and the reproach an obstacle to it. Scripture inverts that. The reward is great in heaven; the leaping is a reasoned response to a fact about the future, not an atmosphere manufactured in the present.
roots_summary: Hebrew dalag (H1801), to leap or spring; pazaz (H6339), to leap or be agile; Greek hallomai (G242), to leap up; skirtao (G4640), to leap for joy.
roots_lines: Hebrew dalag (H1801) — to leap or spring; then shall the lame man leap as an hart (Isaiah 35:6).
Greek hallomai (G242) — to leap up; used of the healed man at the Beautiful gate (Acts 3:8) and of the well of water springing up (John 4:14).
Greek skirtao (G4640) — to leap for joy, used of the babe in the womb (Luke 1:41) and commanded under persecution (Luke 6:23).
Greek brephos (G1025) — a babe, used alike of John in the womb (Luke 1:41) and of Christ in the manger (Luke 2:12).
Greek exallomai (G1814) — to leap up out, the compound opening the account in Acts 3:8.
usage: Then shall the lame man leap as an hart (Isaiah 35:6) — not merely walk, but leap, with the surplus of a creature never lame.
The babe leaped in her womb (Luke 1:41) — the forerunner begins his ministry before birth.
Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy (Luke 6:23) — commanded in the hour of reproach, on the ground of a reward in heaven.

etymology: From back and the Anglo-Saxon suffix -weard, denoting direction. Webster 1828: with the back in advance; toward the back; on the back part. Scripture makes the direction a moral one: to go backward is to apostatize, and the two occasions when men fall backward are both moments of holy dread.
biblical_def: Twice in Scripture men walk backward and it is reverence; once a nation goes backward and it is ruin. Shem and Japheth cover their father without looking: And Shem and Japheth took a garment, and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness (Genesis 9:23). The awkward gait is the whole point — they take deliberate trouble not to see what Ham had gone and told. Against this stands Isaiah’s indictment, where the same direction is covenant treachery: Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity... they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward (Isaiah 1:4). Apostasy in Scripture is rarely a leap; it is a walking away with the face still pointed at the sanctuary. In the garden the arresting party discovers what happens when the divine name is spoken by the One it belongs to: As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground (John 18:6). And Hezekiah is given the strangest sign in the Old Testament: the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward (Isaiah 38:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BACKWARD as with the back in advance; toward the back; on the back part; toward past times; and figuratively, unwilling, averse, reluctant, slow.
webster_full: BACKWARD, adv. — With the back in advance; as, to move backward.
Toward past times or events; as, to look backward on the history of man.
By way of reflection; retrospectively.
BACKWARD, a. — Unwilling; averse; reluctant; hesitating; also, slow; sluggish; dilatory.
From back and -ward, the Anglo-Saxon weard, direction, as in toward, homeward.
scriptures: Genesis 9:23

And Shem and Japheth took a garment, and laid it upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father; and their faces were backward, and they saw not their father's nakedness.
Isaiah 1:4

Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward.
John 18:6
As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground.
Isaiah 38:8
Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down.
corruption_summary: Genesis 9:23 commends men for refusing to look, which cuts directly against the modern conviction that exposure is honesty and discretion is repression.
corruption_paragraphs: Ham saw and told; his brothers walked backward and covered. Scripture blesses the two who declined the information. This is the opposite of the reigning instinct, which treats the uncovering of a father’s shame as candour, authenticity, or overdue truth-telling, and treats the covering of it as complicity. The Bible knows the difference between the sin that must be confronted by the elders and the nakedness that must simply be covered by a son. Charity shall cover the multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8), and love beareth all things (1 Corinthians 13:7). A culture organized around public exposure — of parents, of pastors, of the dead — has mistaken Ham’s posture for virtue. The fifth commandment stands over this text, and so does the curse that followed the telling.

Isaiah 1:4 names the manner of apostasy exactly: gone away backward. Men do not usually renounce the faith; they reverse out of it slowly while still facing the right way. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance is often misheard as a promise that nothing of the sort can happen to a professing believer, but the confession is more careful. Perseverance is the genuine fruit of regeneration, not a guarantee attached to a past decision, and the same Scriptures that promise the elect shall not finally fall warn continually against drawing back. Hebrews 10:38-39 holds both together in a sentence. The bare formula once saved always saved, detached from any expectation of fruit, is not the doctrine of the 1689 Confession, and Isaiah 1 is what it looks like when a whole nation keeps the outward face and moves the feet.
roots_summary: Hebrew achor (H268), the hinder part, backward; nazor (H2114), to be estranged or go away backward; Greek opiso (G3694), backward, behind.
roots_lines: Hebrew achor (H268) — the hinder part; their faces were backward (Genesis 9:23), and the shadow returned backward (Isaiah 38:8).
Hebrew nazor (H2114) — to be estranged, to turn away; they are gone away backward (Isaiah 1:4).
Greek opiso (G3694) — backward, to the rear; they went backward, and fell to the ground (John 18:6).
Hebrew maalah (H4609) — a step or degree, the marks on the dial of Ahaz (Isaiah 38:8).
Hebrew ervah (H6172) — nakedness, shame; the thing covered in Genesis 9:23 and legislated in Leviticus 18.
usage: They went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father (Genesis 9:23) — the awkward gait is the point; they take trouble not to see.
They are gone away backward (Isaiah 1:4) — apostasy walks away with its face still toward the sanctuary.
I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground (John 18:6) — the arresting party meets the divine name and cannot stand.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon stoppian, to close up, to obstruct, ultimately from Late Latin stuppare, to stop with tow. Webster 1828: closed; obstructed; hindered from proceeding. In Scripture two things get stopped: wells, and mouths — and the stopping of the mouth is a courtroom verdict.
biblical_def: Paul’s long argument from Romans 1 to Romans 3 ends not with a conclusion but with a silence: Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God (Romans 3:19). The law’s first office is not to reform the sinner but to silence him. Every excuse, every comparison, every appeal to sincerity is closed off, and the defendant stands with nothing to say. Only from that silence can the next verses speak of a righteousness of God without the law, freely by His grace. David had already sung the same order: the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped (Psalm 63:11). The word is also literal and hostile. Isaac inherits his father’s wells and finds them ruined: all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth (Genesis 26:15) — the enemy’s work is not to build a rival well but to fill in an old one. And men stop their own ears against the word: they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears, that they should not hear (Zechariah 7:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STOP as to close, as an aperture, by filling or by obstructing; to obstruct; to hinder from proceeding; hence STOPPED, closed, obstructed, hindered.
webster_full: STOP, v.t. — To close, as an aperture, by filling or by obstructing; as, to stop a vent.
To obstruct; to render impassable; as, to stop a way or passage.
To hinder from proceeding; to arrest the progress of.
STOPPED, pp. — Closed; obstructed; hindered from proceeding; impeded.
Anglo-Saxon stoppian; Late Latin stuppare, to stop with tow or oakum.
scriptures: Romans 3:19
Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
Psalm 63:11
But the king shall rejoice in God; every one that sweareth by him shall glory: but the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped.
Genesis 26:15
For all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth.
Zechariah 7:11
But they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears, that they should not hear.
corruption_summary: Romans 3:19 makes the stopped mouth the precondition of the gospel, and every preaching method that spares the hearer that silence has removed the ground justification stands on.
corruption_paragraphs: The law’s use in convicting the sinner — what the Reformed tradition calls the pedagogical or second use — is the doctrine Romans 3:19 states. Its practical loss is the most consequential corruption in modern evangelical preaching. Where the hearer is addressed first as wounded rather than as guilty, the mouth is never stopped, and a message of forgiveness arrives for a crime that was never named. The therapeutic vocabulary is precise about this: it can speak at length of what has been done to a man and hardly at all of what he has done before God. But Scripture’s order is fixed. All the world must become guilty before God before the righteousness of God can be received by faith. Remove the first clause and justification becomes an encouragement rather than an acquittal.

Genesis 26:15 describes the standing method of opposition: the Philistines dig no wells of their own, they fill Abraham’s with earth. The pattern holds in doctrine. Error rarely proposes a new source of living water; it stops the old ones with rubbish — a confession left unrecited, a catechism dropped, a text explained until nothing runs. Isaac’s response is the model, and Genesis 26:18 records it: he digged them again, and called them after the names by which his father had called them. That is what confessional recovery is. The 1689 Confession, the catechisms, and the recovery of expository preaching are not innovations but re-digging, and the old names are kept on purpose.
roots_summary: Hebrew satham (H5640), to stop up, to shut; saqar (H5534) and atsam (H6105), to shut fast; Greek phrasso (G5420), to fence in, to stop the mouth; sunecho (G4912), to hold together, to stop the ears.
roots_lines: Greek phrasso (G5420) — to fence in, to block, to stop a mouth; that every mouth may be stopped (Romans 3:19).
Hebrew satham (H5640) — to stop up or shut; used of the wells the Philistines filled (Genesis 26:15).
Hebrew saqar (H5534) — to shut fast; the stopped mouth of liars (Psalm 63:11).
Greek sunecho (G4912) — to hold together; the mob stopped their ears at Stephen’s witness (Acts 7:57).
Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to make heavy or dull, used of ears made heavy against the word (Zechariah 7:11).
usage: That every mouth may be stopped (Romans 3:19) — the law’s first office is to silence the sinner, not to reform him.
The Philistines had stopped them, and filled them with earth (Genesis 26:15) — the enemy fills in old wells rather than digging rival ones.
Stopped their ears, that they should not hear (Zechariah 7:11) — unbelief is an act, not merely a condition.

etymology: From Old French refreschir, to make fresh again, from re- (again) and fresch (fresh). Webster 1828: cooled; invigorated; revived; reanimated. Scripture applies the word once, astonishingly, to God Himself at the close of the creation week.
biblical_def: The most arresting use of this word in the Bible has God as its subject: It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever: for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed (Exodus 31:17). The Almighty does not tire (Isaiah 40:28 says so in as many words), so the language is condescension — God speaking of Himself in terms a creature can feel, in order to ground a commandment the creature must keep. The sabbath is anchored not in human need but in the divine pattern, and the pattern is stated in the warmest available word. Among men the refreshing is ordinary and mutual. David’s company, fleeing Absalom, came weary, and refreshed themselves there (2 Samuel 16:14). Paul, who could be sharp about the churches, is careful to name the men who eased him: they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such (1 Corinthians 16:18). And to Philemon he writes what may be the highest compliment in the epistles: we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother (Philemon 1:7). A man may be measured by whether the saints leave his company rested.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REFRESH as to cool; to allay heat; to give new strength to; to invigorate; to revive after depression; hence REFRESHED, cooled, invigorated, revived, reanimated.
webster_full: REFRESH, v.t. — To cool; to allay heat; as, a shower refreshes the air.
To give new strength to; to invigorate; to relieve after fatigue; as, sleep refreshes the body.
To revive; to reanimate after depression; to cheer; to enliven.
REFRESHED, pp. — Cooled; invigorated; revived; reanimated; cheered.
French refraichir, from re, again, and frais, fresh — the same root as English fresh.
scriptures: Exodus 31:17
It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever: for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed.
2 Samuel 16:14
And the king, and all the people that were with him, came weary, and refreshed themselves there.
1 Corinthians 16:18
For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such.
Philemon 1:7
For we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother.
corruption_summary: Exodus 31:17 grounds the sabbath in six literal days of creation, and both the creation account and the commandment are weakened together when those days are dissolved into ages.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 31:17 is not a poetic aside; it is the reason clause of a commandment, and its logic depends on the days being days. For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested — the human week is commanded because it images the divine one. Exodus 20:11 makes the same argument in the Decalogue itself. This dictionary holds six literal twenty-four-hour days as its position, and this text is a principal reason: a framework that turns the days into ages, epochs, or a literary scheme leaves the fourth commandment resting on an analogy that no longer runs. The old-earth positions held by some in the Reformed line are not confession-breaking and are treated here as tolerable error rather than heresy, but they are not the dictionary’s voice, and Exodus 31:17 is where the cost of them shows.

Philemon 1:7 gives a measure of a man that modern church culture has largely mislaid: the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee. The bowels in Hebrew and Greek idiom are the seat of deep affection, and the compliment is that Philemon’s love left the brethren rested. Note what it is not. It is not that he was impressive, influential, or in demand. The current vocabulary of ministry — platform, reach, brand — measures a man by the traffic he generates, and by that measure a Philemon is invisible. Paul thought it worth writing down. So did the Puritans, whose pastoral theology is full of this: the test of a Christian’s company is what condition the saints are in when they leave it.
roots_summary: Hebrew naphash (H5314), to take breath, to be refreshed; Greek anapauo (G373), to give rest, to refresh; anapsucho (G404), to cool again, to revive.
roots_lines: Hebrew naphash (H5314) — to breathe, to take breath, to be refreshed; used of the LORD on the seventh day (Exodus 31:17) and of weary men (2 Samuel 16:14).
Greek anapauo (G373) — to cause to rest, to refresh; they have refreshed my spirit (1 Corinthians 16:18) and the bowels of the saints are refreshed (Philemon 1:7).
Greek anapsucho (G404) — to cool again, to revive; used of Onesiphorus refreshing Paul in prison (2 Timothy 1:16).
Greek splagchna (G4698) — the bowels, the seat of tender affection, the thing refreshed in Philemon 1:7.
Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, to desist, the root of sabbath and the companion verb to naphash in Exodus 31:17.
usage: He rested, and was refreshed (Exodus 31:17) — condescension in the warmest available word, grounding a commandment in the divine pattern.
They have refreshed my spirit and yours (1 Corinthians 16:18) — Paul names the men who eased him and tells the church to acknowledge them.
The bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother (Philemon 1:7) — a man may be measured by whether the saints leave his company rested.

etymology: From hand and full: as much as the hand will grasp. Webster 1828: as much as the hand will grasp or contain; a small quantity or number. In Scripture the handful is the unit of the memorial offering and the standing measure of God’s sufficiency in famine.
biblical_def: A handful is what is left when everything else is gone, and Scripture keeps putting it at the hinge of the story. The widow of Zarephath states her situation as a death sentence: I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die (1 Kings 17:12). She is asked to give that handful away first, and the barrel does not fail through the famine. The same measure is the appointed portion in the meat offering: he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar (Leviticus 2:2). God takes a handful and calls it the memorial; the rest feeds the priests. The Preacher weighs the handful against the full grasp and prefers it: Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit (Ecclesiastes 4:6). Against all three stands the boast of Benhadad, who reckoned Samaria itself would not yield handfuls for all the people that follow me (1 Kings 20:10) — and who lost.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HANDFUL as as much as the hand will grasp or contain; a small quantity or number; a palmful.
webster_full: HANDFUL, n. — As much as the hand will grasp or contain.
A small quantity or number; as, a handful of men.
A palm; a hand’s breadth; four inches.
As much as the arms can embrace or hold.
From hand and full; compare the Hebrew qomets, the closed hand, the priest’s portion.
scriptures: 1 Kings 17:12

And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.
Leviticus 2:2

And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons the priests: and he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar, to be an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD:
Ecclesiastes 4:6
Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.
1 Kings 20:10
And Benhadad sent unto him, and said, The gods do so unto me, and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people that follow me.
corruption_summary: The Zarephath narrative is a favourite text of the prosperity teachers, who read the widow’s handful as seed sown for a return; the passage is about the sufficiency of God in famine, not a technique for obtaining abundance.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 17 is regularly preached as a transaction: give your last handful to the man of God and God will multiply it back to you. That reading has the direction of the covenant reversed. The widow is not investing; she is obeying a prophetic word in a famine that God Himself had declared, and what she receives is not wealth but daily sustenance — a barrel that does not waste and a cruse that does not fail, exactly enough, for as long as the drought lasts. Prosperity teaching (Hagin, Copeland, and the modern seed-faith industry) turns this into a law of return, and in doing so makes God a mechanism and the giver the real agent. The Reformed doctrine of providence says the opposite: God gives daily bread as He sees fit, and the widow’s security lay in His word, not in the size of her gift. Our Lord Himself cites this very widow in Luke 4:26 — and He cites her as an instance of sovereign election, not of successful giving.

Leviticus 2:2 guards a second point. God requires a handful, not the whole; the memorial portion is burnt and the remainder feeds Aaron’s sons. The token is not a discount on obedience but the appointed form of it, and offering more than commanded is no more acceptable than offering less — Nadab and Abihu are two chapters away. This is the regulative principle in its Levitical form: what God commands is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted, in the offering as in the worship. Ecclesiastes 4:6 then applies the same measure to ordinary life, and the verdict is against the full grasp: a handful with quietness beats two hands full with vexation.
roots_summary: Hebrew qomets (H7062), the closed hand, a handful; kaph (H3709), the hollow of the hand; shoal (H8168), a handful as a measure; malo kaph, the fulness of the palm.
roots_lines: Hebrew qomets (H7062) — the closed hand and so a handful; the priest’s memorial portion of the meat offering (Leviticus 2:2).
Hebrew kaph (H3709) — the hollow or palm of the hand; an handful of meal in a barrel (1 Kings 17:12).
Hebrew shoal (H8168) — a handful as a formal measure, the same word as the hollow of God’s hand in Isaiah 40:12.
Hebrew azkarah (H234) — the memorial, the name given to the handful burnt on the altar (Leviticus 2:2).
Hebrew nachath (H5183) — quietness, rest; the thing that makes the single handful better (Ecclesiastes 4:6).
usage: An handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse (1 Kings 17:12) — the widow is asked to give the last of it away first.
He shall take thereout his handful... and burn the memorial of it (Leviticus 2:2) — God takes a handful and calls it the memorial.
Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail (Ecclesiastes 4:6) — the verdict is against the full grasp.
